public_rationale: The March 2021 shortcut-learning synthesis documents recurring cases where benchmark success failed to transfer to more demanding tests [e1]. The June 2019 HANS study found that four models successful on MNLI performed poorly when syntactic shortcuts gave incorrect answers [e2]. These findings support the qualitative claim that benchmark success can overstate mastery of the intended capability [e1, e2]. However, a June 2019 image-classification study found that accuracy gains transferred to new test sets despite lower absolute accuracy [e3].
limitations: The evidence does not measure how often benchmark gains are misleading across AI [e1, e2, e3].
Failures to generalize do not establish that no genuine improvement occurred; some gains transferred to independent tests [e2, e3].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Improvement on AI benchmarks does not necessarily reflect real progress; such progress is often illusory.

statement.excerpt: The heart of Hoel’ss argument boils down to (my words not his) “AI has done better over time on benchmarks so we must be making progress”; in reality, progress can be and often is illusory.
statement.document_title: The New Sport of Misrepresenting AI Criticism

our_interpretation: The plain reading concerns progress in the capability a benchmark purports to measure. A higher score alone need not establish that progress.
I read 'often' as a recurring, documented problem across research settings. Marcus supplies neither a numerical frequency nor a population of benchmark gains.
The historical scope is AI research through the post date. The wording supplies no starting date.
criteria.support_condition: Research documents recurring cases in which benchmark success depends on shortcuts and does not carry over to independent tests of the intended capability.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence shows that the alleged recurring failures are invalid or isolated, and that the benchmark successes under discussion reliably transfer to independent tests of their intended capabilities.

evidence.publisher: arXiv; author manuscript of a Nature Machine Intelligence perspective
evidence.explanation: The perspective synthesizes a recurring mismatch between benchmark performance and performance under more demanding conditions. It supports the qualitative warning, but supplies no estimate of the fraction of all benchmark gains that are misleading.

Four models scored well on MNLI but generally performed poorly when the tested syntactic shortcuts gave incorrect answers. This establishes a concrete gap between benchmark success and reliable inference.

New CIFAR-10 and ImageNet tests produced lower absolute accuracy, but improvements between models still transferred. This limits any broader inference that benchmark progress generally disappears on independent testing; it does not refute the existence of recurring shortcut failures.
